pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7; rainforests are found in a belt around the middle of the Earth — in South America (the Amazon), Central Africa (the Congo), and Southeast Asia — appearing on every continent except Antarctica and Europe.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 Geography (name/locate continents and oceans; hot places near the Equator) and KS1 Y2 habitats.
• Standards—US: NGSS/early geography — locating regions; K-ESS3-1 (organisms and environment) as context.
• Operational details: build on 'near the Equator' — tropical rainforests cluster in a green belt around the warm middle of the globe. Name the three great blocks (Amazon in South America, Congo in Central Africa, Southeast Asia) and the memorable rule that they grow on every continent EXCEPT Antarctica (too cold) and Europe. Use a globe/world map so 'a belt around the middle' is spatial. Keep it to recognising WHERE, tied to WHY (the warm, wet middle).
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) point to the middle of a globe and say rainforests grow there; Tier B (6) name one rainforest region (Amazon/Congo/Southeast Asia); Tier C (7) explain that rainforests form a belt near the Equator and are missing from Antarctica (too cold) and Europe.
bestPractices: Use a globe or world map so 'a belt around the middle' is a spatial pattern, not a list of names
Connect location to cause — they cluster near the warm, wet Equator — reinforcing the previous topic
Name the three great rainforest blocks with a landmark each (Amazon river, Congo, islands of Southeast Asia)
Make the exceptions memorable: none in Antarctica (too cold) and none in Europe
Point out these are far from most children's homes, seeding the global-connection idea for the foods topic
keyRepresentations: World map with the equatorial rainforest belt highlighted green
Three labelled regions: Amazon (South America), Congo (Africa), Southeast Asia
Globe spin showing the green band circling the warm middle
Continent checklist: rainforests on all except Antarctica and Europe
commonMisconceptions: Rainforests are scattered randomly — they form a belt near the warm Equator
There is only one rainforest (the Amazon) — there are great rainforests in Africa and Asia too
Rainforests grow everywhere, even cold places — not in Antarctica (too cold) or Europe
All rainforests are in South America — the Congo and Southeast Asia have huge ones as well
Rainforests are near where I live — for most children they are far away near the Equator

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, help children learn WHERE tropical rainforests are: a belt around the warm middle of the Earth near the Equator, with the three great blocks being the Amazon (South America), the Congo (Central Africa), and Southeast Asia — and that they occur on every continent except Antarctica (too cold) and Europe (an age-appropriate simplification for tropical rainforests). Tie location to cause (hot and wet near the Equator). A labelled world map or globe makes the spatial pattern concrete; place-the-rainforest games and recall checks support it. Keep location tied to the climate reason, not just a list of names.

activities.title: Tap the Equator belt on a world map
feedback: If a child says a rainforest could be anywhere, point to the Equator belt on the globe: a tropical rainforest needs it hot and wet all year, and many places near the middle are like that.
If a child names only the Amazon, show all three regions across South America, Africa, and Asia so they see the Congo and Southeast Asia too.
Reinforce the exceptions: it is too cold in Antarctica for a rainforest, and Europe does not have a tropical rainforest either.
activities.rationale: Locating regions is a spatial task, so a highlightable map or globe shows 'a belt around the middle' as a pattern rather than a list of names, and connects WHERE to WHY at a 5–7 grain. The optional tap-to-highlight, globe-spin, and lift-the-flap interactions make the pattern and exceptions concrete; they are one effective way to present it, not the only way.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests occur in an equatorial belt, with the three largest blocks in the Amazon (South America), the Congo (Central Africa) and Southeast Asia; they occur on every continent except Antarctica and Europe
KS1 pupils name and locate continents/oceans and identify hot places near the Equator
learnerActions: Look at a world map with a warm Equator line drawn across the middle.
Tap the Equator line and watch green rainforest patches bloom in a band near it (with gaps for oceans, mountains and drier places).

Tap each of the three regions in turn: South America (the Amazon spreads with a giant river), Central Africa (the Congo appears), and Southeast Asia (a scatter of steamy green islands) — each with a one-line label.
Use a globe-spin control to see the green rainforest patches lying in a band around the warm middle of the Earth.
Lift a flap answering 'Which continents have NO tropical rainforest?' revealing Antarctica (too cold) and Europe.
activities.intendedInsight: Rainforests are not scattered randomly: they lie in patches in a band around the warm, wet middle of the planet near the Equator, with three great blocks in South America, Africa, and Southeast Asia, and no tropical rainforest in Antarctica (too cold) or Europe.

activities.title: Place-the-rainforest map game / find the green belt
feedback: If markers land away from the Equator, prompt: rainforests need hot and wet weather, which happens near the middle of the Earth — try nearer the Equator line.
Celebrate placing all three great blocks and link them back to the warm belt.
activities.rationale: Having the child actively construct the placement (dragging or spinning) engages them in building the spatial pattern rather than only viewing it. A labelled visual can convey the pattern economically, so this is a complementary active alternative with a different pedagogical purpose. Efficacy relative to the viewing activity is not established here.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests occur in an equatorial belt, with the three largest blocks in the Amazon (South America), the Congo (Central Africa) and Southeast Asia; they occur on every continent except Antarctica and Europe
learnerActions: Drag to spin a globe and find the green belt around the warm middle.
Play a place-the-rainforest game: drag or place rainforest markers onto South America, Central Africa, and Southeast Asia on a world map.
Say aloud where each region is and why rainforests grow there (hot and wet near the Equator).
activities.intendedInsight: Actively placing the regions builds the location idea and the equatorial-belt pattern through the child's own actions.

activities.title: Check and explain: where and why
feedback: Full: child places rainforests in the equatorial belt across several continents and gives the hot-wet climate reason.
Partial: names one or two regions but can't connect them to the hot, wet belt near the Equator — revisit the Equator line and the climate reason.
Gap: says rainforests can be anywhere, or only knows 'the Amazon' with no location sense — point to the Equator belt and show all three regions.

Target answer: Tropical rainforests grow in a belt around the middle of the Earth, near the Equator — like the Amazon in South America, the Congo in Central Africa, and Southeast Asia — because it's hot and wet there all year; it's too cold at the poles and not warm enough in Britain.
activities.rationale: Recall prompts (point-to-the-region, which-continent) check that the map picture is understood, and the reason question forces the climate explanation rather than mere naming, discriminating the concept child from one who thinks rainforests are 'everywhere' or only 'the Amazon'. These prompts assume the map or globe has already been understood, so pair them with the map activity.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests occur in an equatorial belt, with the three largest blocks in the Amazon (South America), the Congo (Central Africa) and Southeast Asia; they occur on every continent except Antarctica and Europe
learnerActions: Point to where the Equator is on the globe and say whether rainforests are near it or far from it.
Name at least two continents that have large rainforests.
Answer: Why couldn't a tropical rainforest grow at the freezing cold South Pole?
Answer the diagnostic: Could there be a big tropical rainforest at the North Pole, or right here in Britain? Where on Earth do tropical rainforests grow, and why there and not just anywhere?
activities.intendedInsight: A secure answer places tropical rainforests in a belt near the Equator across several continents (Amazon/Congo/SE Asia) AND explains they grow there because it is hot and wet all year — not at the cold poles and not in Britain, where it is too cool.

constraints: Use a globe or world map so 'a belt around the middle' is a spatial pattern, not just a memorised list of names.
Always tie WHERE to WHY: rainforests cluster near the warm, wet Equator — this reinforces the prior 'near the Equator' learning.
Name the three great blocks with a landmark each: the Amazon river (South America), the Congo (Central Africa), and the islands of Southeast Asia.

Make the exceptions memorable: no tropical rainforest in Antarctica (too cold) and none in Europe (a tropical-rainforest simplification for this age band; temperate rainforest does occur in parts of Europe).
Point out these regions are far from most children's homes, seeding the global-connection idea for later food topics.
Recall and pointing checks confirm recognition but do not by themselves elicit the climate reason — include a reason question to probe understanding.

Audio-only discussion cannot let a child point to a place or see the equatorial belt, so for this visual/spatial 'where-is-it' task pair any discussion with a map or globe; dialogue can still support naming regions and stating the hot-wet climate reason.
A spinnable 3D globe can give a mild 'belt around a ball' sense, but a 2D map or globe also conveys the equatorial band clearly; 3D is optional, not required.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims are listed as verified:false in the row; treat curriculum and distribution statements as unconfirmed here.

The original assessment uses 'North Pole' in its correct answer but 'South Pole' in a probe; both are used only as too-cold examples. Harmonised to 'the poles' in learner-facing text, keeping 'Antarctica (too cold)' as the precise continent-level exception. No new verification performed.

The claim that rainforests occur on every continent 'except Antarctica and Europe' is an age-appropriate simplification for tropical rainforests (temperate rainforests do exist in parts of Europe); no new verification was performed, and the simplification is also flagged in the activity insight and constraints.

Original media fit rankings (map vs globe vs 3D vs dialogue) were descriptive catalog preferences; they were softened to scoped affordances and limits with no comparative efficacy or necessity claims asserted.

assess.correctAnswer: Rainforests grow in a belt around the middle of the Earth, near the Equator — like the Amazon in South America, the Congo in Central Africa, and Southeast Asia — because it's hot and wet there all year. It's too cold at the North Pole and not hot and wet enough in most of Britain, so tropical rainforests don't grow in those places.

errorPatterns.pattern: rainforests could be anywhere — no link to the Equator
errorPatterns.nextMove: point to the Equator belt on a globe; a rainforest needs hot and wet, which happens near the middle
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — rainforests can grow anywhere, even at the North Pole
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says a rainforest could be at the poles or anywhere

errorPatterns.pattern: the Amazon is the only rainforest — misses the Congo, Southeast Asia and multiple continents
errorPatterns.nextMove: show three regions on the map across South America, Africa and Asia

responseLevels.gap: Says rainforests can be anywhere, or only knows 'the Amazon' with no location sense.
responseLevels.full: Places rainforests in a belt near the Equator across several continents (Amazon/Congo/SE Asia) and explains they grow there because it's hot and wet all year, not at the poles.
responseLevels.partial: Names one or two rainforest regions but can't connect them to the hot, wet belt near the Equator.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Could there be a big rainforest at the North Pole, or right here in Britain? Where on Earth do rainforests grow, and why there and not just anywhere?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks rainforests are 'everywhere' or only 'the Amazon' misses the Equator belt; the concept child ties location to the hot-wet climate near the Equator. The reason-tier forces the climate reason, not just naming places.
